meta.title: Housing affordability and homelessness, 17 days of posts
meta.subject: housing affordability in Texas — rents and home prices, manufactured and factory-built housing, tiny homes, lot-size and zoning rules, county and city development regulations, NIMBY opposition to new communities, and homelessness policy including encampment bans and housing-first funding
meta.subtitle: Oct 1 to Oct 17, 2026. Each dot is one post with 1K+ views about Texas housing affordability, manufactured housing and homelessness, plus every post repeating an earlier one, in the lane for what it argues. Higher and bigger means more views. White means 90% or more the same words as an earlier post, with a white line back to it. Coloured lines link a post to the post it quoted or replied to. Updated daily.

lanes.label: Cut rules, build more supply
lanes.description: Texas rents and prices are high because zoning, minimum lot sizes, permitting and parking rules block construction, so cities and counties should deregulate and let more homes be built.

lanes.label: Manufactured and tiny homes fix it
lanes.description: Manufactured, modular, factory-built and tiny homes are the fast, cheap route to affordable Texas housing, and rules that restrict them should be loosened.

lanes.label: Blame investors, landlords, developers
lanes.description: Corporate landlords, institutional investors, out-of-state buyers and big developers are driving up Texas rents and home prices and pricing out residents.

lanes.label: Protect neighborhoods, local control
lanes.description: Residents oppose new apartments, subdivisions and manufactured-home communities as threats to neighborhood character, traffic, schools and property values, and defend local and county control over development.

lanes.label: Enforce encampment bans, restore order
lanes.description: Homelessness is a public-safety and disorder problem, so Texas should enforce camping bans, clear encampments and push people into shelter or treatment.

lanes.label: Fund housing-first, not criminalization
lanes.description: Ending homelessness requires funding permanent supportive housing and services, and encampment bans and arrests only move people around without fixing the cause.

lanes.label: Pushback
lanes.description: Posts doubting, mocking, fact-checking or arguing against the dominant framings.

posts.name: Texas Ricky
posts.text:
🚨 Oregon’s 39-Year Warning

Nearly four decades of Democratic governors have turned Oregon into a case study in what prolonged one-party rule actually delivers. Unsheltered homelessness ranks among the highest per capita in the country, with tents and encampments a daily reality in Portland and beyond. Property crime sits near the top of national rankings, so urban centers feel less safe even when overall violent-crime numbers look average. Residents face the nation’s highest individual income-tax burden, paired with some of the weakest job growth and housing costs that have locked younger Oregonians out of homeownership.

Elementary reading scores on the NAEP sit well below the national average despite per-pupil spending in the top tier—proof that more funding alone has not fixed the results. Sanctuary policies add further costs that fall on taxpayers while the core problems of disorder, affordability, and stagnant opportunity remain unsolved. Thirty-nine years of the same priorities produced more tents, higher taxes, and fewer realistic paths to a stable middle-class life. States that chose different trade-offs did not end up in the same place.

#Oregon #Homelessness #Crime #Taxes #Education #OnePartyRule #HousingCrisis

This is the same pattern I’ve reported on in Seattle, Portland and San Francisco and I spent the last week digging into how much the city has been funding these various programs (coming soon).
